title: Bargello bookmark
subtitle: A narrow bookmark in a four-step Florentine wave on 13-count canvas
excerpt: This bookmark is worked in a four-step Florentine wave on 13-count canvas. The finished size is 5 cm wide by 20 cm long. Four graduating shades of one colour produce the characteristic ripple of a Bargello wave pattern.
sourceNotes: Bargello wave pattern based on flame stitch descriptions in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Needlework, Florentine work series (1880s).

glossaryTerms.definition: Another name for Bargello needlepoint: vertical straight stitches stepped across the canvas in a wave or zigzag pattern, traditionally in graduating shades of a single colour.

heroPrompt: A finished needlepoint bookmark in four shades of blue showing a Bargello wave, resting across the open pages of an old book, natural light.

content.text: This bookmark is a strip of 13-count canvas, 26 holes wide by 100 holes tall, worked entirely in a four-step Bargello wave. The wave uses four shades of a single colour: darkest to lightest: with each shade filling two wave rows. The finished strip is backed with ribbon and finished at each end with a folded hem.
What you need

items.label: Canvas
items.value: 13-count mono canvas, cut 10 by 28 cm (leaves a 2.5 cm margin around the 26 by 100 hole design area)

items.label: Thread: shade 1 (darkest)
items.value: Persian wool. Suggested: DMC 930 / Anchor 1035 (dark antique blue). About 2 m

items.label: Thread: shade 2
items.value: Persian wool. Suggested: DMC 931 / Anchor 1034 (medium antique blue). About 2 m

items.label: Thread: shade 3
items.value: Persian wool. Suggested: DMC 932 / Anchor 1033 (light antique blue). About 2 m

items.label: Thread: shade 4 (lightest)
items.value: Persian wool. Suggested: DMC 3752 / Anchor 1032 (very light antique blue). About 2 m

items.label: Backing ribbon
items.value: Grosgrain ribbon, 5 cm wide by 22 cm long

content.text: Palette
Shade 1: DMC 930 / Anchor 1035: dark antique blue
Shade 2: DMC 931 / Anchor 1034: medium antique blue
Shade 3: DMC 932 / Anchor 1033: light antique blue
Shade 4: DMC 3752 / Anchor 1032: very light antique blue
Stretching the canvas

A bookmark strip can be worked in the hand without a frame because the upright Bargello stitches cause minimal diagonal distortion. Roll the unworked section into your hand as you work down the length.
Stitches used
Bargello wave stitch
. Each stitch is upright over four canvas threads. The wave steps up or down two threads between adjacent stitches.
Working method

Find the centre of the canvas strip. Work the first row of the wave in Shade 1 across the full 26-hole width. Each stitch is over 4 threads; step up 2 threads at the wave peak and down 2 threads at the trough.
Work a second row in Shade 1 directly below the first, following the wave outline.
Work two rows in Shade 2, then two rows in Shade 3, then two rows in Shade 4. Return to Shade 1 and repeat the cycle.
Continue until the 100-hole length is complete. The wave cycle repeats approximately every 8 rows.
Block the strip by dampening lightly and pressing under a heavy book for two hours. A bookmark does not need the overnight pin-blocking a larger piece requires.
Finishing

Trim the canvas margin to 1 cm on the long sides. Fold to the back. Fold the short ends to the back and secure. Cut the ribbon to the same length as the worked strip and slip-stitch it to the back, enclosing the raw margins. The
Florentine work
surface stays raised and firm from the row-on-row stacking of the upright stitches.
What to try next
A deeper step count of four instead of two gives a sharper, more dramatic wave: often called the flame stitch variant.
